blocks.text: Among the migratory birds of Alexandria, Forsskål in Descript. Animall. p. 9 also lists the Kurki: "it is also called Vaes araki [إوز أرقي [iwazz arqī] anas vigilans [wakeful duck], which might indeed be a name of the crane, since the crane's vigilance is well known; see Bochart below]. It arrives at Constantinople in October, returns after three months, or, as is reported, passes on to India." But on p. 3 the same Forsskål gives Vaes araki as the name of the duck-goose. Hence Velthusen (in Animadverss. ad Cantic. Hisk., printed in the Symbolae Kilonienses, vol. 2, p. 323 ff.) rightly concludes that one name was common to several birds. Yet that the crane too is called Kurki, كركي [kurkī], by the Arabs is clear at least from the proverb about a cautious man, which Bochart will cite further on: احرس من الكركي [aḥras min al-kurkī] more vigilant than a crane.

Forsskål has the same name among the obscure birds of Arabia, p. VIII: "Ghornak, white; it feeds on gadflies that nest on the backs of oxen." Clearly this bird is not the crane. However, since in the fable of the Pygmies, which Bochart will give us from a certain Arab below, p. 77, cranes are plainly to be understood by غرانيق [gharānīq], I would think that this same name was used of different animals in different regions. In Mauretania a certain species of vulture is called by that name; see Hoest, Descript. regni Fessani et Maroccani p. 298, German trans. Cf. Velthusen loc. cit. p. 321.
On the ancient interpretations see also Michaelis in Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1832.
